text:
Sampled-negative separation does not establish full-catalog retrieval quality: sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation, and very small candidate samples increasingly resemble pairwise AUC ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). A 2024 sequential-recommendation study found that aggregate metrics conceal substantial head/mid/tail differences; negative-sampling choices changed both accuracy and popularity imbalance ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). These findings support checking whether large supplied-negative margins coexist with many higher-scoring catalog competitors.

Practical diagnostic proposal: freeze one NextItNet checkpoint per category; select reproducible training-history prefixes with their next observed training item as target. Use causal, left-padded inputs and the final nonpadding feature. Compare supplied-negative margin and pairwise win rate with chunked exact catalog rank: score eligible items, exclude padding and prefix-seen items while retaining the target, and accumulate competitors outranking it using a documented tie rule. Report rank percentiles, training-prefix HR@10, target-minus-10th-competitor margin, and scores/frequencies of the highest-ranked unobserved competitors. Treat these as potential hard negatives, since unobserved does not imply disliked. Cross-tabulate by target training-frequency bands and prefix-length bands, with counts and uncertainty; optionally measure top-10 popularity concentration. This is a proposed application of the literature, not a published NextItNet-specific protocol. Prefix targets may already have influenced training, so results diagnose fitting and competition, not generalization. Keep them explicitly separate from the unchanged host validation HR@10; fit no additional predictor and use no test data.
